title: Reading differently with ChatGPT: EFL learners’ use of Question-Answer Relationship strategy
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners developed reading comprehension when using ChatGPT together with the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy. The core research question was how learners’ reading comprehension changed through this integration, especially across different QAR levels: locating explicit information, synthesizing across text segments, and making inferences about tone and author intent. The study addresses a practical problem in EFL reading instruction: students often need individualized support with vocabulary, sentence structure, and higher-order comprehension, but traditional instruction may not provide timely, adaptive scaffolding.

The intervention combined structured reading strategy instruction through QAR with guided use of ChatGPT. Students completed five weekly guided reading sessions in which they read texts, answered TOEFL-style comprehension questions, generated their own QAR questions and answers, asked ChatGPT to generate questions, and then compared, revised, and discussed responses through free-form interaction. The study used three rounds of semi-structured interviews across five weeks and analyzed 105 interviews thematically using the QAR framework categories (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You) alongside inductive coding.

Participants were 35 first-year undergraduate students in an academic English program at a university in northern China. They were enrolled in two EFL classes per week and also completed one guided ChatGPT-supported reading practice session per week. Most participants self-identified as low-intermediate in TOEFL-related reading proficiency and had limited prior experience with generative AI. Interviews were conducted in Chinese, transcribed, translated, and coded in NVivo.

The main conclusion is that learners described a developmental progression in comprehension: ChatGPT first helped them identify explicit information and understand vocabulary and sentence structure, then supported summarizing and synthesizing across paragraphs, and finally helped them engage in inferential and interpretive reading about tone, stance, and author intention. Students did not simply accept ChatGPT outputs passively; many used it dialogically to compare reasoning and refine their own understanding. At the same time, participants identified limitations in ChatGPT, including weak handling of polysemous vocabulary, unclear parsing of long sentences, overlong summaries, and sometimes inaccurate inferential explanations. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be a useful reading partner when paired with structured strategy instruction, but its value depends on critical, strategic use and AI literacy.
